section_summary: Pages 74-105 conclude a Japanese Foreign Affairs Association propaganda pamphlet defending Japan’s conduct in the 1937 North China conflict. It describes the Tungchow massacre, blames the Nanking government, Blue Shirts, and Communists for obstructing a local settlement, and includes appendices, military maps, publication advertisements, and extracts concerning the 1927 Nanking Incident. Page 106 is a 1939 State Department cross-reference note concerning an Ecuadorian contract with the Japanese national N. Suzuki for cinchona cultivation and a quinine laboratory.

subfiles.title: How the North China Affair Arose: conclusion, appendices, maps, and publisher’s back matter
subfiles.doc_type: Propaganda pamphlet with appendices, advertisements, and maps
subfiles.about: A Japanese advocacy pamphlet attributes the 1937 North China conflict to Chinese militarism, nationalism, Blue Shirt activity, and Communist influence while presenting Japan as seeking local settlement and cooperation.
subfiles.summary: The surviving text begins with an account of the attack on the Japanese garrison and civilians at Tungchow, including graphic allegations of torture and massacre. It argues that Nanking’s troop movements and rejection of a local settlement expanded the Lugou Bridge crisis, then traces anti-Japanese policy to the Kuomintang, Blue Shirts, and Communists. Appendices reproduce force estimates and statements about the 1927 Nanking Incident, while the concluding material contains a colophon, advertisements for Japanese periodicals and books, a publications list, and maps of Beijing-area maneuver grounds and Chinese army deployments in July and August 1937.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on N. Suzuki’s Ecuadorian cinchona and quinine contract
subfiles.about: The note cross-references a report on an Ecuadorian contract allowing N. Suzuki to cultivate cinchona, establish a quinine laboratory, and import up to eighty technicians and laborers.
subfiles.summary: The Ecuadorian Minister of Agriculture was authorized to contract with the Japanese national N. Suzuki for cinchona planting and a quinine laboratory. The summarized provisions allowed Suzuki to bring no more than eighty technicians and laborers into Ecuador, presumed to be Japanese nationals; the originating item is indexed under file 822.6173 Suzuki, N./2.
